The Honorable Mehmet Oz, M.D., MBA 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
Re: 
Request for Information: Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, 
Orthotics, and Supplies Items (CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
The Access to Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (ACGP) Coalition appreciates the opportunity 
to respond to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) Request for Information 
(RFI) on prior authorization for laboratory tests, set out in Section III.E of the proposed rule 
referenced above. We commend CMS for recognizing that prior authorization, as applied to 
laboratory testing, can operate as a barrier to medically necessary care, and we welcome the 
specific questions on which the agency has invited stakeholder input. 
ACGP is a coalition of leading molecular diagnostics and biopharmaceutical companies 
committed to expanding patient access to comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) and other 
advanced biomarker testing. Biomarker testing is now foundational to precision oncology: it 
guides treatment selection, identifies patients who may benefit from FDA-approved targeted 
therapies and immunotherapies, and informs clinical decision-making at the points in a patient’s 
care where timing matters most. Delays in testing can directly affect treatment decisions, and, in 
some cases, patient outcomes. Our members’ tests are routinely subject to prior authorization, 
and our comments draw on that collective experience. 
ACGP supports evidence-based utilization management and recognizes that prior authorization 
can play a role in confirming that a service meets established coverage criteria. Our concern is 
not with coverage review. It is with administrative requirements that delay or deny medically 
necessary testing without improving clinical decision-making. 
In this letter we provide background on how prior authorization affects the patients who depend 
on comprehensive genomic profiling, and we respond to the laboratory-related questions in the 
RFI. Our recommendations are summarized as follows: 
• 
Prohibit impacted payers from denying coverage for a laboratory test based on prior 
authorization having been sought or obtained after the “date of service” or specimen-
collection date; 
• 
Require impacted payers to accept prior authorization requests and appeals from 
laboratories, consistent with laboratories’ status as recognized providers; 
• 
Require impacted payers to accept test requisition forms (TRFs) as a valid documentation 
of medical necessity; 
1001 Pennsylvania Ave NW | Suite 1300N | Washington DC 20004 | accesstoCGP.com 
 
• 
Require greater transparency and specificity from impacted payers and laboratory benefit 
managers (LBMs) regarding coverage criteria, documentation requirements, denial 
rationales, and outcome metrics; and 
• 
Provide a mechanism for ordering clinicians, patients, and laboratories to notify CMS 
when payers fail to comply with prior authorization rules. 
Background 
Comprehensive Genomic Profiling and Biomarker Testing 
Molecular and genomic testing, hereditary cancer panels, pharmacogenomics, comprehensive 
genomic profiling, companion diagnostics, and minimal residual disease assays operates under a 
distinct coverage regime that includes the Medicare MolDX program, test-specific identifiers, 
technical assessments, and medical policies that can lag current clinical guidelines. 
A large share of clinical decisions is informed by laboratory testing, and in oncology a biomarker 
result frequently determines whether a patient is eligible for a targeted therapy or 
immunotherapy or even a clinical trial, and must be available before the next treatment decision 
is made. In this setting, results of the test can ensure the best therapeutic option. 
Responses to the RFI’s Questions 
ACGP offers the following responses to the questions posed in the RFI. 
1. How do prior authorization requests for laboratory tests currently impact patient care 
and health care provider burden? 
Prior authorization imposes a substantial burden on ordering providers, laboratories, and patients, 
and that burden has grown as authorization has shifted from the exception to the norm. 
Laboratories devote dedicated staff and infrastructure and frequently third-party vendors to 
obtaining documentation, monitoring payer-specific requirements, coordinating with ordering 
offices, responding to denials, and pursuing appeals. None of this work advances patient care. 
The clinical cost is greatest when testing drives a time-sensitive decision. Because specimens 
must be analyzed promptly and clinicians and patients are awaiting results, laboratories often 
perform genomic testing in good faith before authorization is resolved, and then absorb denials 
when authorization was not obtained before specimen collection. The practical effect is to 
discourage timely testing and to place at risk the very results on which a treatment decision 
depends. 
2. What are possible outcomes of more Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs), 
Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, and non-Medicare payers allowing a test requisition 
form (TRF) to be valid medical documentation to show that a laboratory test is reasonable 
and necessary? 
Broader recognition of the TRF would, in combination with other reforms, allow more requests 
to be approved without unnecessary friction. When a laboratory must seek authorization because 
the ordering clinician did not, the TRF is generally the documentation it has, and it frequently 
contains everything a payer needs to confirm that coverage criteria are met. Refusing to accept it 
or refusing to accept physician attestation erects a barrier unrelated to medical necessity and 
forces laboratories to chase duplicative records. ACGP supports recognizing a complete TRF as 
1001 Pennsylvania Ave NW | Suite 1300N | Washington DC 20004 | accesstoCGP.com 
 
part of the medical record and as sufficient documentation when it establishes that applicable 
coverage criteria are satisfied; where the TRF is insufficient, the payer may request the specific 
additional information needed rather than denying the request outright. 
3. How frequently are prior authorizations denied because the request was submitted after 
the specimen was collected? 
Post-collection denials are a recurring problem and, for genomic testing, a structural one. The 
concept of “prior” authorization is frequently incompatible with how biomarker tests are used: 
testing is often ordered after a diagnosis and performed on tissue already collected, so the “date 
of service” precedes the moment the test was contemplated. Payers that refuse to accept a request 
after that date deny coverage on a timing technicality divorced from the clinical question. ACGP 
members report that such denials are common among payers that equate the date of service with 
the specimen-collection date. As noted above, CMS has correctly indicated that using a date-of-
service policy to deny prior authorization is not consistent with MA program rules; the agency 
should clarify and enforce that conclusion across impacted payers. 
4. What impacts have laboratory benefit managers (LBMs) had in facilitating prior 
authorization processes, regulating access, and controlling payment for laboratory 
services? 
Many payers delegate coverage-policy development and utilization management for laboratory 
tests to LBMs. LBMs can add value through structured evidence review, but their involvement 
frequently reduces transparency and increases burden. Coverage criteria, documentation 
requirements, and the identity of the entity responsible for a given policy are often opaque, and 
some policies are treated as proprietary and are not published. When a denial is challenged, the 
payer and the LBM may each attribute the policy to the other, leaving laboratories without a 
clear path to resolution. 
For molecular and genomic testing, LBM policies can impose test-registration or identifier 
requirements, lag behind current clinical guidelines, and apply ordering-specialty restrictions that 
do not reflect how genomic testing is used in practice. ACGP recommends that CMS require 
impacted payers to disclose whether and how a coverage or utilization-management policy is 
administered by an LBM or other third party, identify the entity accountable for the policy, and 
provide an appeal pathway that is not controlled by the same entity that issued the denial. 
5. What opportunities for process improvement exist for prior authorization requirements? 
ACGP recommends that CMS focus on reducing unnecessary administrative burden while 
preserving evidence-based review. In particular, CMS should: 
• 
confirm that laboratories may initiate and manage prior authorization requests and 
appeals for the services they furnish; 
• 
prohibit denials based solely on specimen-collection date or other administrative timing 
requirements; 
• 
direct consistent acceptance of TRFs and physician attestation where they establish 
medical necessity; 
1001 Pennsylvania Ave NW | Suite 1300N | Washington DC 20004 | accesstoCGP.com 
 
• 
require transparency into coverage criteria, denial rationales, responsible entities, and 
appeal pathways; and 
• 
improve oversight of, and accountability for, delegated utilization-management 
programs. 
6. How could automation positively affect patient outcomes and reduce burden? 
Automation can reduce manual effort, speed information exchange, and give providers and 
laboratories real-time visibility into authorization status – but its value depends entirely on the 
policies it implements. Automating a sound process helps; automating a flawed one simply 
produces faster denials. ACGP also cautions that electronic prior-authorization tools designed 
around imaging, procedures, and durable medical equipment do not map cleanly onto laboratory 
testing, which depends on the specific test ordered, LOINC, CPT, and PLA coding, specimen 
type, diagnosis codes, applicable LCD and NCD criteria, and reflex logic. Automation will 
reduce burden for laboratories only if the underlying data fields and coverage rules are built for 
laboratory workflows. 
7. What other issues exist that technology is not currently addressing? 
Many of the most significant problems are matters of policy, not technology. No portal can cure 
inconsistent application of coverage criteria, undisclosed policies, restrictions on laboratory 
participation in the authorization process, or denials premised on collection-date timing. Several 
issues also sit outside the RFI’s current framing: post-payment recoupment and audit-driven 
retroactive denials, which can arrive months or years after a service is furnished; standing-order, 
reflex, and protocol-driven testing, for which a per-patient, pre-service authorization model is a 
poor fit; multi-party reference-laboratory arrangements in which the testing laboratory is not the 
entity holding the payer relationship; and the reality that, for some testing, medical necessity 
cannot be established until a preliminary result is in hand. ACGP encourages CMS to address 
these through clear policy direction, oversight, and accountability. 
8. How do the issues associated with prior authorization impact the health care workforce 
and retention of skilled health care professionals? 
Prior authorization diverts substantial clinical and laboratory capacity away from patient care. 
Physicians, laboratory professionals, genetic counselors, and billing and administrative staff 
spend significant time assembling documentation, tracking requests, and resolving denials and 
appeals—follow-up work that is a well-documented contributor to professional burnout. 
Reducing unnecessary authorization burden would return skilled personnel to the work that 
improves patient outcomes. 
Recommendations 
Drawing on our members’ experience, ACGP offers the following recommendations to improve 
prior authorization for laboratory testing. 
• 
Prohibit denials based on the “date of service” or specimen-collection date. CMS 
should make clear to MA organizations and other impacted payers that equating the date 
of service with the specimen-collection date may not be used to deny coverage for a test 
for which authorization was sought or obtained after that date—consistent with the 
agency’s own statements in the RFI preamble and with 42 C.F.R. § 422.138(b). CMS 
1001 Pennsylvania Ave NW | Suite 1300N | Washington DC 20004 | accesstoCGP.com 
 
should communicate this through rulemaking and sub-regulatory guidance, monitor 
compliance, and direct that a request for authorization be accepted at any time before 
timely claim submission. 
• 
Require impacted payers to accept prior authorization requests and appeals from 
laboratories. Consistent with 42 C.F.R. § 422.566(c)(1)(ii), CMS should enforce that an 
MA plan must accept a request from a laboratory as a recognized provider, and should 
extend the same expectation to other impacted payers—allowing either the laboratory or 
the ordering clinician to submit and check the status of a request, regardless of network 
status. 
• 
Require acceptance of TRFs as a part of medical necessity documentation. CMS 
should explicitly require that a completed TRF is part of the medical record and is 
sufficient documentation when it contains the clinical information needed to determine 
medical necessity, and that additional records may be required only where the TRF is 
insufficient. 
• 
Require granular transparency from payers and LBMs. Metrics aggregated at the 
organization level have little practical value. CMS should require reporting broken down 
by requesting-provider type, by denial reason, and by ultimate claim disposition where 
authorization was sought, and should require payers to disclose whether and how each 
policy is administered by an LBM and which entity is accountable for it. 
• 
Provide a non-compliance reporting mechanism. CMS should establish a publicized 
process through which clinicians, patients, and laboratories can report payer non-
compliance with prior authorization rules, together with a resolution path for systemic 
problems that the ordinary, claim-by-claim appeal process cannot practically address. 
Conclusion 
ACGP appreciates CMS’s attention to the burden that prior authorization places on laboratory 
testing and on the patients who depend on it. We support prior authorization programs that are 
transparent, evidence-based, operationally workable, and focused on facilitating appropriate care. 
For comprehensive genomic profiling and biomarker testing, the stakes are high: these tests 
determine whether patients can access the targeted therapies and immunotherapies that define 
modern oncology care (including access to clinical trials), and authorization practices that delay 
or deny them on administrative grounds bear directly on patient outcomes. 
We respectfully urge CMS to prohibit date-of-service and collection-date denials, confirm 
laboratories’ ability to initiate authorization requests and appeals, and require acceptance of 
TRFs and meaningful transparency from payers and LBMs. We thank CMS for the opportunity 
to comment and welcome the chance to serve as a resource as the agency develops these policies. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Access to Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (ACGP) Coalition
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Access to Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (ACGP) Coalition
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group / Industry Coalition
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Coalition of molecular diagnostics and biopharmaceutical companies focused on expanding patient access to comprehensive genomic profiling, biomarker testing, companion diagnostics, hereditary cancer panels, pharmacogenomics, and related advanced tests.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ACGP responds to the RFI on prior authorization for laboratory tests and supports evidence-based utilization management only when it does not delay or deny medically necessary genomic and biomarker testing. The coalition asks CMS to prohibit date-of-service/specimen-collection denials, require payers to accept laboratory-submitted PA requests and appeals, accept test requisition forms as documentation, improve payer/LBM transparency, and create a non-compliance reporting mechanism.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL/RFI laboratory testing; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; TRANSPARENCY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS by analogy; API-USAGE-METRICS by analogy.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 42 C.F.R. § 422.138(b); 42 C.F.R. § 422.566(c)(1)(ii).
- **Standards referenced:** LOINC; CPT; PLA coding; LCD/NCD criteria; electronic prior authorization tools; laboratory benefit managers.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prohibit specimen-collection/date-of-service denials**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI laboratory testing
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Biomarker and genomic testing may be ordered after diagnosis and performed on tissue already collected; denying PA because authorization occurred after the collection date is a timing technicality unrelated to medical necessity.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit impacted payers from denying coverage solely because PA was sought or obtained after the date of service or specimen collection.

**Topic 2: Laboratory ability to submit PA and appeals**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI laboratory testing
- **Position:** Modify/Clarify
- **Rationale:** Laboratories frequently furnish the service and hold relevant documentation, yet payer rules can prevent them from submitting or managing PA and appeals.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to accept PA requests, status checks, and appeals from laboratories as recognized providers, regardless of network status.

**Topic 3: Test requisition forms as documentation**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; GENERAL/RFI laboratory testing
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** TRFs often contain the clinical information needed to determine medical necessity; refusing them creates duplicative records-chasing.
- **Specific request:** Require acceptance of complete TRFs as part of the medical record and sufficient documentation when they establish applicable coverage criteria.

**Topic 4: LBM and payer transparency**
- **Provision ID:** TRANSPARENCY; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** LBM policies can be opaque, proprietary, lag clinical guidelines, impose test identifiers, or create unclear accountability between payer and LBM.
- **Specific request:** Require disclosure of coverage criteria, documentation requirements, denial rationales, responsible entities, appeal pathways, and reporting by provider type/denial reason/claim disposition.

**Topic 5: Automation must fit laboratory workflows**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** ePA tools designed for imaging, procedures, and DME may not map cleanly to lab workflows involving test, code, specimen type, diagnosis, policy, and reflex logic.
- **Specific request:** Build automation around laboratory-specific data fields and coverage rules; do not simply automate flawed policies.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S66-S82:** Directly responds to the RFI on laboratory tests, especially impacts on patient care, TRFs, post-collection denials, LBMs, process improvement, automation, technology gaps, and workforce impact.
- **S16/S17:** Recommends granular denial rationales, documentation requirements, and accountable entities.
- **S29/S35:** Recommends reporting broken down by requesting-provider type, denial reason, and claim disposition rather than only organization-level metrics.
- **S20/S21:** By analogy, emphasizes that timing rules must not delay time-sensitive oncology testing.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Prohibit denials based on date of service or specimen-collection date.
2. Require impacted payers to accept PA requests, status checks, and appeals from laboratories.
3. Require acceptance of complete TRFs as part of medical necessity documentation.
4. Require transparency into payer and LBM coverage criteria, documentation requirements, denial rationales, responsible entities, and appeal pathways.
5. Create a non-compliance reporting mechanism for clinicians, patients, and laboratories.
6. Ensure automation is built for laboratory workflows, including LOINC, CPT, PLA, specimen type, diagnosis codes, LCD/NCD criteria, and reflex logic.
7. Address post-payment recoupment, retroactive denials, standing/reflex testing, reference-lab arrangements, and situations where medical necessity depends on preliminary results.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Administrative timing denials, inability of labs to participate fully in PA, rejection of TRFs, opaque LBM policies, and automation of flawed processes.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed oncology treatment decisions, denial of medically necessary testing, provider/lab burden, appeals, financial exposure, and reduced access to clinical trials or targeted therapies.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Laboratory-specific coding and coverage complexity, third-party LBM policies, network-status issues, payer opacity, and non-lab-oriented ePA tools.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No numerical data; cites members' collective experience that post-collection denials are common among payers using collection-date policies.
- **Studies or research referenced:** References Medicare MolDX, LCDs, NCDs, and clinical guidelines generally.
- **Examples provided:** Oncology biomarker testing, companion diagnostics, minimal residual disease assays, tissue already collected before test order, LBM test-registration and identifier requirements.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients needing oncology testing, ordering clinicians, laboratories, genetic counselors, payers, LBMs, and biopharmaceutical/molecular diagnostics companies.
- **Economic implications:** Labs may absorb denials for good-faith testing; administrative work requires dedicated staff and vendors.
- **Technical feasibility:** Automation is feasible only if designed for lab-specific fields and workflows.
- **Patient care impact:** High, because genomic/biomarker results often determine targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or clinical trial eligibility.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / Concerned
- **Tone:** Detailed; technical; policy-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Automating a sound process helps; automating a flawed one simply produces faster denials." - Context: Warning about technology without policy reform.
2. "Post-collection denials are a recurring problem and, for genomic testing, a structural one." - Context: Explains the date-of-service concern.
3. "A biomarker result frequently determines whether a patient is eligible for a targeted therapy or immunotherapy or even a clinical trial." - Context: Patient-access rationale.
4. "Refusing to accept [a TRF] or refusing to accept physician attestation erects a barrier unrelated to medical necessity." - Context: Support for TRF acceptance.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - PA requires clinicians and labs to chase records, manage denials, and pursue appeals.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Delays can affect oncology treatment selection and trial access.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Lab workflows require specific data elements not always supported by generic ePA tools.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong emphasis on payer/LBM criteria, denial rationales, appeal pathways, and metrics.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Laboratory testing often involves specimens, reflex logic, and multi-party arrangements not compatible with pre-service PA.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Discusses LBMs and third-party administrators of coverage policies.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requires coordination among labs, clinicians, patients, payers, and LBMs.
